segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then shall we say? Should we remain in sin so that grace may increase?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Absolutely not! We who died to sin, how can we still live in it?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So we were buried with him through baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if we have become joined to him in the likeness of his death, we will certainly also be joined to him in the likeness of his resurrection.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We know this: our old self was crucified with him so that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would no longer be slaves to sin;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for the one who has died has been justified from sin.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: knowing that Christ, raised from the dead, dies no more; death is no longer his master.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the death he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life he lives, he lives to God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the same way, you too must count yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So do not let sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and do not present the parts of your body to sin as weapons of unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as people who are alive from the dead, and the parts of your body to God as weapons of righteousness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For sin will not be your master, since you are not under law but under grace.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then? Should we sin because we are not under law but under grace? Absolutely not!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do you not know that when you present yourselves to someone as slaves, to obey him, you are slaves of the one you obey, whether of sin, leading to death, or of obedience, leading to righteousness?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But thanks be to God that you, who were slaves of sin, obeyed from the heart the pattern of teaching to which you were handed over,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and, set free from sin, you were enslaved to righteousness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am speaking in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented the parts of your body as slaves to impurity and to lawlessness, leading to more lawlessness, so now present the parts of your body as slaves to righteousness, leading to holiness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For when you were slaves of sin, you were free with regard to righteousness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So what fruit did you have then from the things you are now ashamed of? For the outcome of those things is death.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But now, set free from sin and enslaved to God, you have your fruit, leading to holiness, and the outcome is eternal life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

notes.note: The Greek is a two-word wish, literally 'may it not be', which Paul uses to reject a false inference in the strongest terms. The older 'God forbid' adds a word the Greek does not have, and 'by no means' is now rather faint. The same phrase recurs in verse 15.

The adjective describes things that have grown together, such as a graft and its stock or the edges of a healing wound. The Greek has no 'him': it can also be read as 'grown together with the likeness of his death', with the likeness itself as the thing believers are joined to. Most translations supply 'with him', as here. The second 'joined to him in the likeness of' is supplied from the first half of the sentence, where the Greek says only 'of his resurrection'.

notes.traditional: our old man / our old self
notes.note: Literally 'our old human being'. After the contrast between Adam and Christ in the previous chapter, a first reader would probably hear this as the person one was as a member of Adam's humanity, not as one part of the personality. 'The body of sin' likewise means the body as sin's possession and instrument, not that the body is evil in itself.

Most translations switch to 'freed' here, but the verb is the one translated 'justify' throughout Romans, and it is kept so the reader can see the link. The sense is legal: someone who has died is cleared of sin's claim. Many scholars think 'freed' or 'acquitted' is all that is meant, perhaps echoing a maxim that death settles every debt. Greek has one word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice, justify).

The word can mean tools in general, but in the plural it ordinarily meant arms, and that is its sense everywhere else in Paul's letters. The military picture fits the passage: sin 'reigns' and is a 'master', and in verse 23 it pays a soldier's wages. Many translations keep the more neutral 'instruments', which is also possible.

notes.phrase: the pattern of teaching to which you were handed over
notes.traditional: that form of doctrine which was delivered you
notes.note: One would expect teaching to be handed over to people, and some older versions translate that way, but the Greek says the people were handed over to the teaching. The image is probably that of a slave transferred to a new master, in keeping with the surrounding verses. The 'pattern' is the mould or standard of instruction that shapes those placed under it.

The noun can name the process of being made holy, that is, set apart for God, or the resulting state. 'Sanctification' is the traditional word and stresses the process; 'holiness' is used here as plainer English, but the Greek does not decide between the two. The same word occurs in verse 22.

notes.phrase: from the things you are now ashamed of?
notes.traditional: What fruit had ye then in those things whereof ye are now ashamed?
notes.note: Ancient manuscripts had no punctuation, and the sentence can be divided differently: 'So what fruit did you have then? Things you are now ashamed of.' The translation follows the punctuation of the Greek edition used, which is also that of most English versions. Either way the point is that the old life yielded nothing worth having.

The adjective is formed from the word for 'age'. In Jewish usage 'eternal life' is the life of the age to come, so the phrase describes a kind of life as well as an unending one. 'Eternal' is the standard translation; a minority of translators prefer 'life of the age to come'.

The word was the usual term for a soldier's pay or ration allowance, which continues the military imagery of verse 13. Sin is pictured as a commander paying what has been earned, and that pay is death. God, by contrast, does not pay wages but gives a gift, a word in Greek closely related to 'grace'.

candidates.reason: Translations vary between 'slave', 'servant' and 'bondservant' across the New Testament, and the choice changes how readers hear both social references and Paul's self-descriptions.
Paul's uses range from physical body to human frailty to the sphere opposed to the Spirit, and versions vary between 'flesh', 'human nature' and 'sinful nature'; a single policy is needed.
A frequent Pauline verb rendered variously as 'destroy', 'abolish', 'nullify' or 'render powerless', with real theological consequences depending on the choice.
It recurs in Paul, Hebrews and 1 Peter, and translations vary between 'sanctification', 'holiness' and 'consecration'; it should also be coordinated with ἅγιος and ἁγιάζω.
A key verb in Romans 4 and elsewhere ('reckon', 'count', 'credit', 'consider', 'impute'); readers should be able to see that the same word is used here as in the argument about Abraham.
